description: A step-by-step process of building simple, smart digital solutions for the NASA Space Apps Challenge.
summary:
We reached other worlds. But what did we leave behind?

ABANDONED BUT NOT FORGOTTEN is an interactive digital archive and virtual museum dedicated to humanity's forgotten explorers across the Solar System.

From the Apollo Lunar Modules to the Mars rovers and distant spacecraft, the project brings together the stories of machines that explored other worlds, completed their missions, and left their mark behind.

Through interactive exploration, historical information, real mission imagery, and 3D spacecraft models, visitors can discover what remains, understand what these explorers achieved, and explore their lasting scientific legacy.

Their missions ended. Their stories didn't.
details:
The project addresses an important gap in how humanity's space exploration history is presented and preserved. Thousands of machines and scientific instruments have traveled beyond Earth, yet information about their locations, missions, discoveries, and remaining traces is scattered across different sources.

Our solution is a digital archive that brings these stories together in one accessible and interactive experience.

The website features six main sections:

• THE HUMAN FOOTPRINT: Discover humanity's physical presence beyond Earth.

• WHAT IS STILL THERE: Explore the objects and equipment that remain on other worlds.

• MISSION ARCHIVE: Learn about the history, objectives, and achievements of exploration missions.

• SPACECRAFT GALLERY: Explore spacecraft and scientific equipment through images and interactive 3D models.

• PLANETARY EXPLORER: Discover the celestial bodies connected to these missions.

• SCIENTIFIC LEGACY: Understand the discoveries and knowledge these missions contributed to science.

The collection covers 13 categories of historic spacecraft, rovers, landers, and scientific equipment, creating a unified experience that connects exploration history with interactive digital storytelling.
